question: How do you summarise a posterior and simulate predictions by working with samples from it instead of integrals?
hypothesis: Working with posterior samples turns calculus problems into counting and data-summary problems, and generalises to MCMC output.

limits: Only the one-parameter globe tossing model; multi-parameter cases are deferred to later chapters.
Chapter has no benchmarks: all numbers are toy illustrations and sample-dependent (no seed except set.seed(100) in practice problems).
Intervals: author says 95% conventions are arbitrary and the true-value coverage is a small-world number.
The year and edition are not printed in the extracted pages.
practices: Work with samples from the posterior rather than integrals; counting samples in an interval gives the posterior mass (sec 3, p51-54).
Use percentile intervals for roughly symmetric posteriors and HPDI for skewed ones; if the choice matters, plot the whole posterior (p56-57).
Prefer 67%/89%/97% nested intervals over a default 95% (Rethinking box, p58).
You rarely need a point estimate; if you do, pick a loss function: absolute loss gives the median, quadratic loss gives the mean (p58-61).
Propagate parameter uncertainty by drawing predictions from posterior samples (rbinom(..., prob=samples)); plugging in one point estimate is overconfident (p64-66).
Check models with several summaries of the data (longest run, switches), not only the one the model uses (p67-68).
Simulate dummy data to validate software, design research and forecast (p61-62).
Present base-rate problems in natural frequencies (counts) to make them intuitive (p50).

PI( samples , prob=0.5 )
HPDI( samples , prob=0.5 )
